\[
a = 1 - \frac{\bar I(c)}{255},
\quad
\operatorname{area}\left(\text{disk}(\rho) \cap \text{cell}\right) = a\, s^2,
\quad
I'(p) = 255 \left(1 - \operatorname{clamp}\left(\rho - |p - c| + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\right),
\qquad s = 8,\ \theta = 45^{\circ}
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(a\): The ink share of a cell
- \(\bar I(c)\): The box mean of the image at the cell center
- \(\rho\): The dot radius
- \(s, \theta\): The cell size and the screen angle

The screen is a grid of square cells of side s, turned by theta. The darkness a of a cell is one minus the box mean of the image at the cell center c. The box has about the cell's size, and it is read by bilinear interpolation. The dot is a disk centered at c whose area inside the cell is a s^2. Above a quarter of pi, about 0.785, the disk passes the sides of the cell. Then its radius rho comes from the area of a circle cut by a square, solved by bisection. Each pixel is black inside the dot and white outside, with one pixel of anti-aliasing at the edge. So a flat gray keeps its mean tone. These rules are PixelNexus's own. Ulichney's book covers halftoning in depth.
